segments.t: In managed environments an administrator can restrict or preconfigure korTTY through a single TOML file, KTPH000, placed in the installation directory. Users cannot change or bypass it: the file is only read from the admin-writable installation folder, locked settings appear grayed out with a "Managed by your organization" hint, and hand-editing KTPH001 is undone on the next load. This chapter explains where the file lives, how rules target users, groups and servers, and documents every available parameter with examples.
Without a KTPH000 nothing changes — korTTY behaves exactly as before. The shipped KTPH001 is a fully commented template with everything disabled.

korTTY loads the policy exclusively from the KTPH000 folder of its installation directory — the folder that also holds the application jar — and never from KTPH001 or any other user-writable location. A ready-to-copy template ships as KTPH002; copy it to KTPH003 in the same folder and restart korTTY (there is no hot reload).

The enforcement model relies on the operating system's file permissions: the installation directory must be writable only by administrators, which is the default for the locations above. korTTY additionally logs a warning when the active policy file is writable by the current user. During development (never in a packaged installation) a policy can be tested with KTPH000.

If the file exists but cannot be parsed or contains an invalid value, korTTY starts in a fail-safe lockdown: every policy-controllable feature is denied, no server connection is allowed, every terminal paste with a line break asks for confirmation, programs cannot put text on the clipboard with OSC 52, the previous session is not reopened at startup, the output of terminal panes is not saved for it, and a startup dialog names the file and the exact error position. A typo can therefore never silently disable enforcement. One invalid rule rejects the entire file; unknown keys only produce log warnings, so a policy written for a newer korTTY does not lock out users of an older version.

Rules target the current OS login name (matched lowercase). Group membership comes from two sources at once: groups defined in the policy's KTPH000 table, and the user's OS-level group memberships. On domain-joined Windows machines the OS groups include Active Directory groups, so rules can target AD groups directly — both fully qualified (KTPH001) and as the bare name (KTPH002) — without any directory server configuration.

Each KTPH000 block optionally names KTPH001 and/or KTPH002; a rule naming neither applies to every user. Per setting, the most specific tier that sets it wins: KTPH007user beats group beats everyoneKTPH008. That is the familiar group-policy pattern — lock everything down in a baseline rule for everyone, then relax individual settings for a trusted group. When several rules of the same tier set the same key, the most restrictive value applies (KTPH003 over KTPH004 over KTPH005 over KTPH006); for server rules, a connection must pass every applicable restriction of the winning tier. The order of rules in the file has no significance.

The KTPH000 table restricts which servers a user may connect to — as an allow-list (KTPH001: only listed servers are reachable) or a deny-list (KTPH002: listed servers are blocked). The restriction is enforced centrally for every connection path: saved connections, QuickConnect, split panes (to a new connection or the same server), session restore, SFTP, teamwork-shared connections, AI swarm targets and scheduled jobs, including the jump host of a connection. Blocked connections stay visible in the connection manager but are grayed out with a lock marker, and any connect attempt shows a clear policy message.

KTPH000Open GroupKTPH001 in Quick Connect skips every connection of the group whose server or jump server is blocked and names them all in one policy message; the other connections of the group still open. KTPH002ConnectKTPH003 in the Connection Manager, a tab's KTPH004DuplicateKTPH005 and KTPH006Reopen Closed TabKTPH007 check the policy before they ask for a password, a temporary SSH key or the master password, and an open tab checks it again on every connect and reconnect attempt, because editing a saved connection also changes the tabs already opened from it. If such an edit points a tab at a blocked server or jump server, its terminal shows the policy message and korTTY stops trying, including automatic reconnects.

Patterns match the host string exactly as configured in the connection — korTTY never resolves DNS for policy checks, so host names and IP addresses are separate namespaces: if a server is reachable both ways, list both.
KTPH000 = any characters, KTPH001 = one character
IPv6 ports require the bracket form
Rejected (lockdown) when this korTTY does not understand the version
Shown in every "Managed by your organization" hint and dialog
Defines a policy group; rules referencing the name target its members. OS/AD groups match automatically and need no entry here
Optional label used in log messages
Targets the listed OS login names (user tier)
Targets members of policy groups and/or OS/AD groups (group tier); a rule with neither KTPH000 nor KTPH001 applies to everyone
Allow-list or deny-list semantics for KTPH000
Master switch: KTPH000 disables every AI capability at once, and scheduled AI Agent and AI Swarm jobs end as blocked before they connect
AI Agent (menu, terminal context menu, keyboard shortcut, headless job runs). KTPH000 also blocks scheduled AI Agent and AI Swarm jobs before they connect, because swarm agents are AI agents
AI chat, Saved Chats and the terminal-selection AI actions
AI Swarm, including scheduled swarm jobs, which end as blocked before they connect
Teamwork shared-connections sync (service is not started, menu locked)
Plugin loading and the Plugins menu (e.g. terminal effects)
The KTPH001session journalKTPH002: capture, journal bar, manager, viewer and exports. Not chained to KTPH000 — with AI denied the journal still records raw activity

The KTPH003control APIKTPH004 and its KTPH000 client: KTPH001 stops the listener, locks the Settings checkbox and forces the setting off. Not chained to KTPH002 — the API is local automation, not an AI capability

KTPH002Highlight rules that actKTPH003 when their pattern appears in terminal output (a desktop notification, or KTPH004running a snippetKTPH005 in the pane): KTPH000 stops every such action, also a snippet the user already allowed for a connection, locks KTPH006Run actions of highlight rules (notifications, snippets)KTPH007 in KTPH008Settings → TerminalKTPH009 in the off position and keeps the rule editor from giving a rule an action. Keyword highlighting itself is not affected. KTPH001 locks the setting on

Typing into several terminals at once: KTPH002multi-execKTPH003 across tabs and windows and a tab's broadcast mode. KTPH000 locks the include items of KTPH004View → Multi-execKTPH005, KTPH006View → Panes → BroadcastKTPH007, the Multi-exec and Broadcast Mode entries of the tab, pane and Dashboard context menus, and their command palette and shortcut entries; no pane can join from anywhere. KTPH008Stop Multi-execKTPH009 and switching broadcast mode off keep working. There is no Settings control, so KTPH001 changes nothing

Copying files between this computer and a server. KTPH000 greys out the KTPH006SFTP managerKTPH007's KTPH008UploadKTPH009 and KTPH010DownloadKTPH011 buttons and the transfer list's KTPH012RetryKTPH013, rejects drags onto either panel that would copy to or from the server, stops server files being dragged out of the window, rejects files dragged onto a terminal pane while they are dragged, greys out the Snippet Manager's KTPH014Copy as file(s) to terminal directoryKTPH015 and KTPH016Copy folder to terminal directoryKTPH017 for SSH tabs, greys out the upload and download buttons of the terminal's KTPH018remote files sidebarKTPH019 and rejects drops onto it and drags out of it, and makes the JobScheduler's SFTP upload, download and sync actions and its rsync action fail with the policy message before they connect. Opening the SFTP manager (also with KTPH020Open SFTP HereKTPH021 on a terminal's session), browsing (also in the remote files sidebar) and remote-only operations (rename, delete, permissions, owner, archives, search, remote copy) keep working, and loading a file into the snippet editor stays under KTPH001. KTPH022Edit in External EditorKTPH023 needs a local copy, so KTPH002 greys it out too. Commands such as KTPH003 or KTPH004 typed into a terminal cannot be blocked by korTTY. There is no Settings control, so KTPH005 changes nothing

KTPH006Editing server files as rootKTPH007 from the SFTP manager. KTPH000 greys out KTPH008Edit as Root (sudo)...KTPH009 in the right-click menu and the remote KTPH010EditKTPH011 menu. It is also greyed out while KTPH001 is denied or KTPH002 is KTPH003 or KTPH004, because an edit as root always needs a local copy and always writes back. There is no Settings control, so KTPH005 changes nothing

KTPH000 forces interactive approval of every mutating command set and defeats the auto-approve option; KTPH001 lets the agent plan and chat but never execute commands. Scheduled jobs: under KTPH002 an KTPH007AI Agent or AI Swarm jobKTPH008 blocks every server-changing command, whatever its KTPH009Auto-approve AI commandsKTPH010 says, because nobody is there to approve it; under KTPH003 both AI job types end as blocked before they connect. A job is also blocked up front when KTPH004 or KTPH005 is denied, and a swarm job when KTPH006 is denied
Naming a feature takes it over, whichever way you decide it

A policy file that mentions a key locks the corresponding control, in the position the policy chose. Writing KTPH000 therefore locks the checkbox KTPH002onKTPH003 — users can no longer switch the API off themselves. Leave the key out entirely to leave the choice with the user; write KTPH001 to take it away.
Forces the master-password gate at startup; the setting is locked
SSH host key verification cannot be disabled anywhere — globally, per group or per connection — and trusted host keys cannot be removed or replaced in korTTY
Forbids terminal session recording, including the session-level toggle

Never opens the KTPH000SSH tunnelsKTPH001 configured on connections (local, remote and dynamic port forwarding); the tab's status bar says they are disabled by your organization. A jump server hop is not affected
KTPH000 confines korTTY to its own in-memory clipboard — see below

Programs in a terminal can never put text on the clipboard with OSC 52, whatever KTPH001Settings → TerminalKTPH002 says: the setting is forced off and KTPH003Let programs in the terminal copy text to the clipboard (OSC 52)KTPH004 is locked with the "Managed by your organization" hint, and korTTY checks the policy again on every write. KTPH000 leaves the choice, which is off by default, to the user and locks nothing
Users cannot add teamwork sources; only KTPH000 entries remain
Users cannot create script headers; only KTPH000 entries remain
Upper bound for the script text stored with each Full code analysis; KTPH000 forbids storing script text — see below
Users cannot create AI profiles (buttons and wizard are locked)
Users cannot edit their existing AI profiles either
Forbids every AI internet-access mode — see below
KTPH000 cuts AI web access at three levels

The KTPH000internet accessKTPH001 dropdown of an AI profile selects a
web-search or MCP browsing backend. Forbidding it is enforced in three places, because a single
one would leave a gap:

KTPH001Stored settingsKTPH002 — every profile's mode is reset to KTPH003DisabledKTPH004 whenever the settings are
   loaded or saved, so a value from before the policy arrived does not survive, and neither does
   a hand-edit of KTPH000.

KTPH000The interfaceKTPH001 — the dropdown is locked with the "managed by your organization" hint in
   both the AI Manager and KTPH002Settings → AIKTPH003.

KTPH000Every AI requestKTPH001 — korTTY refuses to build a service for a profile whose mode is enabled,
   which closes the window between two clamps. The request fails with a policy message rather
   than quietly answering without the web tool the profile asked for.

This is about the search backends only. It does not stop a KTPH002cloudKTPH003 AI profile from reaching its
own provider — for that, deny the KTPH000 feature or provision KTPH001 entries that point
at an internal endpoint.

A KTPH002Full code analysisKTPH003 stores the script text it worked on — the analysed script, the text an apply started from, the proposed result and the accepted text — so the code preview, KTPH004View changesKTPH005, the script export, the report appendix, KTPH006Restore intermediate stateKTPH007 and resuming after a restart keep working. Users choose the size themselves under KTPH008Settings → Snippet Editor → Stored script size per analysisKTPH009 (default 1 MB, maximum 5 MB, or KTPH010OffKTPH011); KTPH000 in KTPH001 is an upper bound on top of that choice:

KTPH000Effective limitKTPH001 — The smaller of the user's own value (default 1 MB), the fixed 5 MB maximum and this key. A value above 5 MB therefore changes nothing, and a user's lower value stays in force. Any positive value is accepted, also one below the 256 KB minimum users can pick.

KTPH001KTPH000KTPH002 — No script text is stored at all: the analysis keeps its findings, summary, diagram and reports, but not the script, so KTPH003View changesKTPH004, the older entries' code preview, the script export, the report appendix, KTPH005Restore intermediate stateKTPH006 and resuming after a restart are unavailable, and the panel says the organization does not allow storing script text. The analysis itself, applying findings and the immediate change review in the editor work as before. Text stored earlier is dropped from the stored analyses the next time they are written.

KTPH001Settings dialogKTPH002 — The dropdown only offers sizes up to the cap, shows the cap beneath it and is locked (with the "Managed by your organization" hint) when the value is KTPH000. The user's own choice is not overwritten by the cap: it applies again when the policy is lifted.

KTPH002TiersKTPH003 — Like every setting the most specific tier that sets the key wins (user, then group, then all); rules of the same tier take the smaller value, so KTPH000 beats every positive cap. The key is not a KTPH001-means-unlimited value.

KTPH002Invalid valuesKTPH003 — A negative number or a non-integer (for example KTPH000) is a policy error like any other malformed value, so the whole file is rejected and the lockdown fallback applies; the fallback forbids storing script text too. Write bytes, optionally with TOML digit separators (KTPH001).
No llama.cpp/MLX runtime downloads or update checks
The Hugging Face model browser and downloads are disabled
Only admin-provisioned KTPH000 entries can be loaded by embedded AI profiles
Disables the automatic update check and the manual check in the About dialog
Update checks query this endpoint instead of GitHub; it must return the same JSON shape as the GitHub KTPH000 API (KTPH001, KTPH002 with KTPH003 and KTPH004)

KTPH000 keeps loading remote files into the snippet editor but forbids writing back to the target system; KTPH001 removes the feature entirely, including opening file paths and KTPH002 links from terminal output (KTPH007Links in terminal outputKTPH008). The same mode applies to server files in the KTPH009SFTP ManagerKTPH010: KTPH003 opens them without KTPH011Overwrite fileKTPH012 and KTPH013Save as...KTPH014, and KTPH004 disables KTPH015Edit in Snippet EditorKTPH016 and KTPH017Open imageKTPH018 for them; local files are not affected. KTPH019Edit in External EditorKTPH020 follows the same mode: KTPH005 opens the file without uploading saves, and KTPH006 disables it

The least a KTPH004paste warningKTPH005 may ask. It is a floor, applied on top of KTPH006Settings → Terminal → Paste protectionKTPH007, a connection's own paste warning and the paste warning of a teamwork connection, so none of them can ask less often; one that asks more often keeps doing so. The stored setting is raised to the floor, and the dropdown carries the "Managed by your organization" hint and offers only the floor and stricter choices; with KTPH000 it is locked. When several rules of the same tier set it, the stricter value wins (KTPH001 over KTPH002 over KTPH003)

Sets what korTTY does at startup with the previous session's windows and tabs (KTPH004Settings → Window → KTPH005Session RestoreKTPH006KTPH007) and locks the dropdown. KTPH000 reopens nothing by itself; KTPH008File → Restore Previous SessionKTPH009 stays available. When several rules of the same tier set it, the value that opens fewer connections by itself wins (KTPH001 over KTPH002 over KTPH003)

Sets and locks KTPH003Also restore the output of each terminal pane (encrypted)KTPH004 in KTPH005Settings → Window → KTPH006Session RestoreKTPH007KTPH008, together with KTPH009Lines of output per paneKTPH010. KTPH000 switches it off, which deletes the output saved so far at the next start; KTPH001 switches it on, and the output is still saved only while a master password exists and the vault is unlocked. When several rules of the same tier set it, KTPH002 wins

The most files the SFTP manager copies at once. A cap on KTPH000Parallel transfersKTPH001 in KTPH002Settings → KTPH003SFTP ManagerKTPH004KTPH005: a higher stored value is lowered to it and the spinner goes no higher, while users may still choose fewer. With KTPH000 korTTY detaches from the operating system clipboard entirely and uses its own in-memory clipboard instead: text copied in another application cannot be pasted anywhere in korTTY, and text copied in korTTY never reaches the OS clipboard — while copy, cut and paste KTPH001withinKTPH002 korTTY keep working everywhere, because terminals, SFTP views, the snippet editor and all dialogs share the same internal buffer. Because this is pure application logic and no OS clipboard isolation API is involved, it behaves identically on macOS, Windows and Linux, including the X11 primary selection (middle-click paste): pasting middle-click content from other applications is blocked, middle-click paste of korTTY-internal copies keeps working.

The mode covers the terminal (shortcuts, context menu, middle-click, text dropped onto it from another application, which is refused, and text that a program in the terminal copies with OSC 52 where KTPH001Settings → TerminalKTPH002 allows it, which lands in the internal clipboard only), the code editor, all copy buttons, the KTPH000 snippet variable, and the copy/cut/paste shortcuts of plain input fields. Copying images (AI-generated pictures, diagram exports) is unavailable in internal mode, since an image can only be shared via the OS clipboard.

The internal clipboard is a policy tool against casual data transfer through the clipboard, not a hard air gap: a user can still read text on screen. The right-click KTPH000PasteKTPH001 entry of plain text fields is provided by the UI toolkit and may still access the OS clipboard — the keyboard shortcut and every korTTY-provided menu are covered.
An AI profile's API key never appears in plain text in the policy. The administrator encrypts it once from a terminal — the command prints a KTPH000 value for the KTPH001 key:
Users see only "API key provided by your organization" in the profile; the key is decrypted in memory at the moment a request is made.

The envelope uses AES-256-GCM with an application-wide key, so it protects against casual disclosure (shoulder surfing, config diffs, backups) and detects tampering — it is not hard secrecy, since anyone with the korTTY binary could recover the application key. The installation directory's OS permissions remain the actual security boundary; prefer per-user keys via the normal profile flow when that boundary is not enough.
